title: An Ignatian day at home
hookLine: morning offering, finding God in work, examen at night

lines: AN ALARM, A KETTLE, LOST SHOES.
NO RETREAT HOUSE. JUST A WEEKDAY.
cards: The alarm goes off. Feet on a cold floor, a kettle, a phone already buzzing, someone who can't find their shoes. No retreat house, no director, no month of silence.
Just a weekday. Lately this path has walked through the Spiritual Exercises and the Jesuits who live by them.

Today is the last day with them, and it asks a practical question: what does all of that look like in an ordinary house, with dishes in the sink? One Ignatian answer comes in three pieces: morning, middle and night.

teach.b: An Ignatian day at home. Piece one, the morning offering. Before the day runs away, a short prayer hands it to God in advance: the prayers, the work, the joys, the sufferings.
One familiar version was spread by a prayer movement founded by a Jesuit, and it comes in more than one wording. It's the Suscipe in miniature: take, Lord, receive, today.
Piece two, the middle of the day: God in all things. No extra hour of prayer required.

The laundry, the commute, the email, the child's question become places to notice God at work, the way the young Jesuit student learned to find God over his grammar book. Contemplatives in action, at the kitchen sink.
Piece three, the examen at night, which you first met on day two hundred thirty-seven.

teach.h: THE WHOLE JESUIT WAY, IN ONE DAY.
teach.b: Tradition says Ignatius would let a busy Jesuit shorten other prayers, but not this one.
In the Exercises he lays it out simply: give thanks for the day's gifts, ask for light, go back over the hours, ask pardon where you fell short, and look toward tomorrow with hope.
It takes a few minutes, and needs no words aloud.

teach.h: THY MERCY IN THE MORNING, THY TRUTH IN THE NIGHT.
teach.b: The psalm in the Douay-Rheims holds both ends of the day together: "To shew forth thy mercy in the morning, and thy truth in the night."
And look who has come along these weeks: the foundation, indifference, the two standards, discernment, the Suscipe, cura personalis, the magis, the Salvadoran Jesuits, Pedro Arrupe, a Jesuit pope.
All of it fits into one ordinary day. Tomorrow, a different school of prayer, on a mountain.

how: Catholics shaped by Ignatian spirituality begin the day with a morning offering, try to notice God through the day's work, and end it with the examen before sleep.

games.q: what does “an ignatian day at home” mean?
o: a morning offering, God in the day, the examen at night
a weekend retreat made at home instead of a retreat house
a house blessing a Jesuit gives a family's new home

games.q: an Ignatian day — tap the pairs.
p: mercy in the morning, truth in the night

s: Ignatian prayer only works on a long retreat
a morning offering, God in all things and the examen fit into one ordinary day.
in the Exercises, thanks for the day's gifts comes first.
the examen is only a list of sins
it starts with thanks, asks for light, reviews the day, asks pardon and looks to tomorrow.

games.q: it's late, you're tired, and you've skipped prayer all day. what does the Ignatian way suggest?
o: give up: the day is lost.
do a short examen before sleep.
make up for it with an hour of prayer.
games.why: Ignatius treated the examen as the prayer not to skip. a few honest minutes at night gathers up the whole day.

practice: Look back over the last day: find one thing to be grateful for and stay with it, then ask for light to see the day honestly.

Walk back through the hours, noticing where you felt close to God or to goodness and where far away, and if something needs forgiving, say so simply. Last, look toward tomorrow; if you pray, do all of it in God's company.

wordCard.voice: An Ignatian day at home. A morning offering, God in all things through the day, and the examen at night: the Jesuit way, fitted into an ordinary house. Today's word, and the last of the Jesuits.

carryVoice: Your line: God in all things. Morning, middle and night, in one ordinary house. I'll be here tomorrow.
